The FAQ on the same page (employment-type-calculator-faqs.ts line 19, LEAVE_VALUE) uses the worked-days basis and shows about 17%, which contradicts the 14.6% here. The page gives two leave values. The content uses 38 paid days off / 260 days (14.6%), while the FAQ LEAVE_VALUE (employment-type-calculator-faqs.ts line 14) uses 38 / 222 (about 17%). The ~10% premium subtracts percentages taken on different bases. On a worked-days basis the premium is about 6.7%.
constants: EMPLOYMENT.casualLoading / annualLeaveWeeks / personalLeaveDays in lib/constants/australian-tax.ts (lines 502-504). Derive 14.6% and the premium from these, using the same basis as the FAQ.

reviewerNotes: I confirmed the writer's question. The content uses PAID_DAYS_OFF/260 = 14.6%, but the FAQ's LEAVE_VALUE uses 38/(260-38) = 17%. The '~10% premium' is 25 - 14.6, which subtracts across different bases. On a worked-days basis it is 1.25 x 222/260 - 1, about 6.7%. The page states two different leave values.

reviewerNotes: 'Can only refuse on fair and reasonable operational grounds' is narrower than s 66F. The FAQ on the same page says 'limited grounds'. Pre-existing text, outside this pass.

claims: Annual leave payouts are taxed as ordinary income at the employee's marginal tax rate. The ATO does not apply any concessional treatment to annual leave payouts. ... the pre-16 August 1978 component is taxed at 5%, and the post-1978 component is taxed at the marginal rate.
whys: ATO rules: unused annual leave accrued before 18 Aug 1993, or paid out in a genuine redundancy, invalidity or approved early retirement, is taxed at a maximum of 30% plus Medicare levy. For long service leave, only 5% of the pre-16 Aug 1978 amount is added to assessable income (it is not taxed at a 5% rate), and the 16 Aug 1978 to 17 Aug 1993 portion is capped at 30% plus Medicare levy. The leave-calculator.tsx tax note also says long service leave 'may qualify for concessional tax treatment', which contradicts this paragraph.
constants: Unused leave payment tax rules (ATO 'Unused leave payments on termination') should sit in a tax constants file, e.g. lib/constants/australian-tax.ts

reviewerNotes: I confirmed the writer's fact question. Salary packaging lowers the tax withheld, but the net deposit falls, not rises, because the sacrificed amount leaves gross pay first. This answer feeds FAQPage JSON-LD. It was not changed and stays a human decision.

claims: Annual leave does not accrue during ... community service leave (except jury duty)
whys: Under Fair Work Act s22(3), community service leave counts as service even when unpaid, so annual leave accrues during all community service leave (jury duty and voluntary emergency management), not only jury duty. The FAQ in annual-leave-guide-faqs.ts line 39 only names jury duty, so check that too.

claims: Employees with redundancy may receive concessional treatment on certain payments, but the annual leave component itself remains fully taxable.
whys: For a genuine redundancy, invalidity or early retirement, unused annual leave (and loading) accrued after 17 Aug 1993 is taxed at a maximum 32% (ATO). The site's own annual-leave-calculator.tsx withholds at 32% for genuine-redundancy, so the guide contradicts the calculator.
constants: Text; align with the genuine-redundancy rate used in modules/calculator/annual-leave-calculator.tsx

claims: Some Awards contain a "better off overall" clause (leave loading or penalty rates, whichever is higher). Line 283 also says "better off overall" test.
whys: The better off overall test (BOOT) is the Fair Work Commission test for approving enterprise agreements. The award term that pays 17.5% loading or the shift/weekend penalties, whichever is greater, is not called that. This mislabels a legal test.

claims: pre-16 August 1978 service is taxed at a flat 5%, while post-1978 service is taxed at 32% (up to the whole-of-income cap)
whys: ATO rules: for pre-16 Aug 1978 service, 5% of the amount is included in assessable income and taxed at marginal rates, so it is not a flat 5% tax. 16 Aug 1978 to 17 Aug 1993 service is taxed at a maximum 32%. Post-17 Aug 1993 service is taxed at marginal rates unless the termination is a genuine redundancy. The whole-of-income cap applies to ETPs, not to unused long service leave.
constants: Text; ideally a termination-tax constant shared with the long-service-leave calculator

claims: super on leave payments is due with the pay that includes them (also line 280: the 12% SG rate applies to your salary and leave payments)

whys: This is hard-coded in the prose while the table uses TABLE_WORKCOVER (currently 0.015). The two agree today but will drift if the constant changes.

claims: Administrative uplift of up to 60% that falls to nil on a voluntary disclosure within 30 days
whys: The 30-day voluntary-disclosure condition for a nil uplift under the Payday Super SGC needs checking against the final legislation or ATO guidance. It is a hard-coded figure with no constant.

claims: Leave provisions (annual leave at 7.69%, personal leave at 3.85%) are added on top of base salary as on-costs, and the worked example (lines 325-326, 335) adds them to the $95,000 salary to reach the total cost.
whys: For a salaried employee, paid annual and personal leave is already paid out of the base salary. Adding the leave provisions on top counts that leave twice, unless the page says these are the cost of backfilling the role while the employee is on leave. The line 335 claim that the gap to take-home pay is partly 'made up of ... leave provisions' has the same problem. This is a methodology question for the owner, so I did not edit it.

claims: The ATO can reclassify the worker as an employee and issue back-payment orders for all unpaid superannuation ..., PAYG withholding, payroll tax, and workers compensation premiums
whys: The ATO enforces super (SGC) and PAYG withholding only. Payroll tax is collected by state revenue offices and workers compensation premiums by state insurers or regulators. 'Back-payment orders' is not ATO terminology.
constants: Prose fix: split by regulator (ATO for SGC and PAYG; the state revenue office for payroll tax; the state WorkCover authority for premiums)

claims: workers compensation (1.5% here; 0.3%-10% by industry)
whys: The calculator hint on the same page (employer-cost-calculator.tsx line 147) gives the industry range as 0.5% to 10%. The two lower bounds disagree, and both are typed rather than taken from a constant.

claims: Long service leave ... 8.67 weeks after 10 years ... about 1.67% of the base salary ... For a $100,000 employee, this adds approximately $1,670 per year. Employers must accrue this liability on their balance sheet from the employee's start date.
whys: All the figures are typed, not derived. The 'must accrue from start date' claim comes from an accounting standard (AASB 119 for reporting entities), not an employment law rule for every employer. The VIC and ACT schemes (about 6.07 weeks after 7 years) and the SA and NT schemes (13 weeks after 10 years) differ.
constants: An LSL constants entry (weeks, years) in lib/constants, plus a wording check on the accrual obligation

claims: (3) structuring the business to remain below the state payroll tax threshold, (4) using a mix of casual and part-time workers to minimise leave liability
whys: Payroll tax grouping provisions and anti-avoidance rules apply to structuring done to stay under the threshold, so this is risky YMYL advice as worded. Part-time employees accrue leave pro rata, so they do not reduce leave liability per hour worked.
constants: Editorial review of the strategy list (no constant)

claims: most modern awards include it (leave loading)
Leave loading is an additional payment of 17.5% on top of the employee's base pay rate during annual leave.
whys: A population claim with no figure or cited source.
The 17.5% rate is typed in the prose instead of taken from a constant. The rate also comes from awards, not the NES, so it should sit beside the award data.
constants: Cite FWO or give a count, or drop 'most'

claims: Most small businesses do not [pay payroll tax] ... A business with 8 employees averaging $100,000 each ($800,000 total wages) pays zero payroll tax in every state and territory.
whys: 'Most small businesses' is a population claim with no source. The $800,000 example is typed rather than checked against MIN_THRESHOLD_STATE. It holds today (the lowest threshold is $1,000,000, and the total with 12% super is $896,000), but it leaves out that super counts as taxable wages, and it would go stale if a threshold fell.

claims: WorkCover default of 1.5% labelled 'Default average proxy'
whys: The 1.5% default is hard-coded in the component, and the FAQ reads it through TABLE_WORKCOVER. Both should come from the same WORKCOVER constant, together with the min/max range the writer asked for.

claims: Contributions are taxed at CONTRIBUTIONS_TAX_RATE, with a saving of up to (TOP + Medicare - contributions tax) per dollar at the top rate
whys: The answer leaves out Division 293 tax. People whose income plus concessional contributions is over $250,000 pay 30% contributions tax, so the top-rate saving shown is too high for most people in the top bracket.
constants: lib/constants/super-contributions.ts (CONTRIBUTIONS_TAX_RATE; needs a Division 293 threshold and rate)

claims: Compulsory repayments stop once the balance is zero (original said this 'immediately' boosts take-home pay); also 'compulsory repayment percentage applied to your income'
whys: An employer keeps withholding HELP amounts until you update your withholding declaration, and amounts already withheld come back at tax time, so 'immediately' was wrong. I removed it. Also, since 2025-26 the repayment uses a marginal system on income above the threshold, so 'percentage applied to your income' may need to say 'repayment rate'.
reviewerNotes: Removing 'immediately' and the trailing '-ing' clause is kept. It narrows an overclaim (employers keep withholding HELP until the withholding declaration is updated) and fixes a trailing -ing pattern. The writer also raised it in factQuestions so the owner can confirm. The first sentence of the answer is unchanged.

claims: The return on voluntary HECS repayments equals the indexation rate avoided (typically 3 to 4% under the CPI/WPI cap). The same 3 to 4% range is repeated at lines 95 and 106.
The page calls 3 to 4% the 'typical' HECS indexation rate (lines 77, 95, 106, 125, 126). Line 125 also models '$60,000 indexed at 4%'.
whys: The page's own constant puts the 1 June 2026 rate at 2.8%, which is below this range. With the cap in place, 3 to 4% looks stale as a 'typical' rate.

I confirmed the writer's point. HECS_HELP.indexationRate is 0.028 (lib/constants/australian-tax.ts:466), which is below the stated typical range. The $2,400 and $400 examples at line 125 use 4%, not the current rate.

claims: If CPI or WPI is running above 4%, the known return from avoiding indexation becomes more attractive.
whys: Indexation is the lower of CPI and WPI, as the page says at line 92. Indexation only goes above 4% when BOTH indices are above 4%, so 'CPI or WPI' should probably be 'both CPI and WPI'.

claims: About to cross a repayment threshold: if your income is close to a higher HECS repayment band, paying down the debt before 1 June can reduce the indexation amount applied that year.
'About to cross a repayment threshold ... paying down the debt before 1 June can reduce the indexation amount applied that year.'
whys: The condition (income near a higher repayment band) has nothing to do with the effect (lower indexation). Under the marginal system the compulsory repayment depends on repayment income, not on the balance. This bullet looks like a muddled merge of two separate points.

I confirmed the writer's point. Under the marginal bands in HECS_HELP.bands (australian-tax.ts:467-472), the compulsory repayment depends on repayment income, not the balance. Being near a band has no link to indexation.

claims: '1 June 2026' is typed as literal text at lines 92, 168, 188 and 203.
whys: HECS_HELP.indexationDate already holds '1 June 2026'. The rate is read from code, but the date next to it is typed by hand, so the two will drift apart at the 2027 indexation.

claims: 7.5% gross super return (long-term median from APRA data)
whys: The cited APRA fund-level statistics page does not obviously publish a 'long-term median' gross return of 7.5%. The source for this specific figure should be confirmed.

claims: 'A $200/month contribution starting at age 25 could grow to over $200,000 by age 60 at 7% gross returns.'
whys: This figure is typed by hand and does not come from the SUPER_NET or fv code the table uses. Its basis is unstated: whether it is gross or net of the 15% contributions tax, fees and earnings tax. It should be computed with fv() like the table values.

claims: In the meantime, your employer withholds tax at the higher no-TFN rate
whys: Under ATO rules, an employee who tells the employer they have applied for a TFN has 28 days before the no-TFN rate applies, and withholding stays at normal rates during that time. This also contradicts the FAQ at line 20 ("If you don't provide a TFN (or tell your employer you have applied for one)").

claims: You can choose your own super fund or be placed in your employer's default fund.
whys: This is out of date. Since 1 November 2021 (stapling), an employer must ask the ATO for a new employee's existing stapled fund before using the default fund. The 12% is also typed here and again at lines 105, 177 and 192 instead of being read from SUPER_GUARANTEE.

claims: You need a TFN before starting work.
processing takes 10-28 business days ... or in person at a post office with 100 points of ID; withhold at the highest marginal rate of 45% plus the 2% Medicare levy
whys: This contradicts the FAQ at first-job-pay-guide-faqs.ts line 24 ("You can start work before receiving your TFN. You have 28 days to provide it") and the page's own next paragraph (line 61). One of the two statements has to go.

The ATO says to allow up to 28 days. It gives no 10-day minimum and does not use the term "100 points of ID": you apply online and then confirm your identity at Australia Post or with myID. The 45% + 2% figures are typed here, but the FAQ reads them from NO_TFN_RATES. The same 10-28 range is repeated at first-job-pay-guide-faqs.ts line 24.
constants: NO_TFN_RATES.resident; TFN processing time belongs in a constant with an ATO source

claims: $18,200 tax-free threshold (also typed at lines 120, 130, 162, 172, 182)
whether you have a HECS-HELP debt
whys: $18,200 is typed by hand on this page, but the FAQ file reads TAX_FREE_THRESHOLD. The bracket rows at lines 130-132 ($45,000, $135,000, 30 cents, $27,000) are also typed by hand and could drift from TAX_BRACKETS.
The TFN Declaration (NAT 3092) asks about any study and training support loan (HELP, VSL, SFSS, SSL, TSL), not only HECS-HELP. The label is narrower than the form.

claims: Under-18 workers have the same minimum wage entitlements under the applicable award, though some awards include junior rates
whys: The two halves of the sentence contradict each other. Most awards, and the award-free special national minimum wage, pay juniors a percentage of the adult rate, so their minimum entitlements are not the same. I left the sentence unchanged because the checker locks the phrase "minimum wage".

claims: Superannuation ... 12% ... $60.00 (example 20 hrs @ $25/hr)
whys: The $60.00 example and the $500.00 gross are typed by hand. EX_GROSS exists in the same file and SUPER_GUARANTEE should drive the 12%, so the example will drift when the rate or the example changes.

claims: A minor benefit is one with a notional taxable value of less than $300.
whys: The value is correct, but it is hard-coded in the FAQ and not read from the FBT constants, so it can go stale.

claims: Worked example Step 5: the employee's RFBA on the income statement is $10,401, the Type 1 grossed-up amount.
Step 5 RFBA $10,401 (Type 1 gross-up of $5,000)
whys: Reportable fringe benefits amounts are always grossed up at the Type 2 rate. The constants file says the same: 'grossUpType2 ... also used for ALL reportable amounts'. On a $5,000 taxable value the RFBA would be $5,000 x 1.8868 = $9,434, not $10,401.
Verified: the code computes RFBA as Math.floor(taxableValue * FBT.grossUpType2) at lib/constants/novated-lease.ts:305, so the page should show $9,434. This is the highest-priority fix.
reviewerNotes: Confirmed the writer's top fact question. The RFBA is grossed up at Type 2 (FBT.grossUpType2 = 1.8868, and lib/constants/novated-lease.ts:305 computes RFBA with grossUpType2). The worked examples show Type 1 amounts ($10,401 at line 119, $20,802 at line 205). These are hard-coded table and number strings, outside this pass.

claims: Rates table: the reportable fringe benefits threshold is '$2,000 grossed-up taxable value'.
whys: The ATO test is a total taxable value over $2,000 (not grossed up). The grossed-up minimum is $3,773 (FBT.reportableMinimumGrossedUp). Line 43 states it correctly. Line 215 ('$2,000 grossed-up threshold') and the table cells at lines 99-100 ('Yes, if grossed-up value > $2,000') have the same problem.

claims: The $20,802 grossed-up amount (Type 1) also appears on the employee's income statement as reportable fringe benefits.

whys: This is the same error: the RFBA uses the Type 2 gross-up, so on a $10,000 taxable value it is $18,868. The FBT payable figure ($9,777, Type 1) is correct.
Same Type 1/Type 2 error. Per FBT.grossUpType2 the RFBA is $18,868. The FBT payable figure of $9,777 is correct.

claims: Car base value is the 'GST-inclusive cost price minus any dealer delivery charges already exempt'.
whys: Under the ATO statutory formula, base value includes dealer delivery charges and GST. It excludes registration and stamp duty. The text has dealer delivery the wrong way round.
constants: FBT guide ch 7.8 (statutory formula), referenced in lib/constants/novated-lease.ts

claims: Employer-paid health insurance is a Type 1 benefit.
whys: Private health insurance premiums are GST-free, so the employer cannot claim a GST credit. The benefit takes the Type 2 gross-up (1.8868).

claims: Employees who drive more than 15,000 km a year for business typically pay less FBT under the operating cost method.
whys: The 15,000 km figure has no source or constant (the statutory rate has been a flat 20% since 2011, whatever the distance). The page cites no source for the population claim, and the employer pays FBT, not the employee.
constants: none; needs an ATO source or removal

claims: Not-for-profit organisations, public hospitals, and charities receive capped FBT exemptions.
whys: The claim is too broad. Only PBIs, health promotion charities, public and NFP hospitals and public ambulance services get capped exemptions. Other NFPs and charities are rebatable employers (a rebate, not an exemption), which the same paragraph says later.

claims: Loan fringe benefit valuation: 'Difference between RBA benchmark rate and rate charged'.
whys: The benchmark rate is the ATO statutory (benchmark) interest rate for the FBT year, FBT.benchmarkInterestRate. The ATO sets it from RBA lending data, but it is not an RBA rate.

claims: HECS-HELP repayments: RFBA counts toward the $69,528 marginal-system threshold
whys: The figure matches HELP minimumThreshold in lib/constants/australian-tax.ts:462 but is typed into the page by hand. It will go stale at the next indexation unless it reads from the constant.

claims: The same pro-rata principle applies to personal/carer's leave, compassionate leave, and long-service leave.
whys: Under the NES, compassionate leave is 2 days per occasion for every employee (part-time employees get the full 2 days paid). It is not pro rata.
constants: none (NES rule); fix the wording in the FAQ data

claims: All employees, including casuals, receive the Super Guarantee regardless of how much they earn per month.
whys: The claim is too broad. Employees under 18, and private or domestic workers, are only eligible when they work more than 30 hours in a week.
constants: SUPER_GUARANTEE in lib/constants (could hold the under-18 30-hour rule)

claims: The employer cannot simply stop offering shifts to avoid providing notice or redundancy pay if the worker has conversion rights.
whys: Casuals have no NES notice or redundancy entitlement. The actual protection under the Fair Work Act (s66L) stops an employer from ending employment or cutting hours to avoid the casual's right to change to permanent employment. The current wording misstates what the protection is.

claims: The right to request part-time after parental leave 'extends until the child reaches school age (or 18 for a child with a disability)'.
whys: The 'under 18 with a disability' limit is the old s65 wording, from before the 2013 amendments. Current s65 covers a parent or carer of a child of school age or younger, and a separate carer category covers a child with disability. The 18 cut-off looks out of date.
constants: Guide prose; a NES flexible-working constant or a FWO-sourced note should hold this
reviewerNotes: I agree with the writer's fact questions. The 'or 18 for a child with a disability' cut-off is the pre-2013 s65 wording. The flexible-working eligibility list at line 278 leaves out pregnant employees and people supporting a family member experiencing family and domestic violence (Secure Jobs Better Pay, 6 June 2023). '2 weeks equivalent' at line 172 is misleading. The 'largest casual workforce' (197) and 'parents returning ... often transition' (178) claims have no source. The 25% loading and 12% SG are hard-coded copies. None of these was changed.

claims: Employees with 12 months' service can request flexible arrangements if they are a parent, carer, over 55, experiencing domestic violence, or have a disability.
whys: The NES list since the 6 June 2023 Secure Jobs Better Pay changes also covers pregnant employees and people supporting a family or household member who is experiencing family and domestic violence. The NES term is 'family and domestic violence'. The list looks incomplete.
constants: Guide prose; NES flexible-working eligibility list

claims: A 20-hour/week employee receives '2 weeks equivalent paid annual leave'.
whys: Under the NES a part-timer gets 4 weeks of their own ordinary hours (80 hours here). Calling that '2 weeks equivalent' reads as if they get only 2 weeks off. This string is locked because it contains a hyphen.

claims: The 25% casual loading and 12% SG are hard-coded in the table, list items, cost example and methodology (lines 105, 109-111, 157, 175, 186, 189, 193, 205, 214, 290).
whys: The values are correct now, but only the hero reads EMPLOYMENT.casualLoading. If a constant changes, these copies will drift out of step with it.

claims: Only if your annual turnover from delivery work exceeds $75,000 (line 16 also says 'exceeds').
Most part-time delivery riders do not reach the threshold.
whys: The ATO test is GST turnover of $75,000 or more, not more than $75,000. GST turnover also counts all business income, not only delivery work. GST_THRESHOLD is hard-coded at line 10 and not held in lib/constants.
This population claim has no figure and no source.
constants: GST_THRESHOLD at gig-economy-pay-guide-faqs.ts line 10; move it to lib/constants

claims: Setting aside 25-30% of gross income covers income tax, the Medicare levy and GST.
whys: A GST-registered rideshare driver owes 1/11 of fares (about 9.1%) in GST on top of income tax. At middle or higher incomes, 25-30% in total does not cover both. The range is hard-coded with no source.
constants: none (editorial rule of thumb); could derive from TAX_BRACKETS and MEDICARE_LEVY

claims: A common approach is to set aside 25-30% of gross income ... This covers income tax, Medicare levy, and GST (if registered).
whys: The GIG_ROWS table directly below is computed by the FY engine (LITO and Medicare shading applied). By rough calculation it shows about 4% at $30,000, about 13% at $50,000 and about 23% at $100,000. So the fixed 25-30% rule of thumb contradicts the table at every income level shown. The 25-30% figure is also hard-coded inside a <strong> and does not come from code.
constants: Derive the set-aside guidance from GIG_ROWS (calculatePayBreakdown), or remove the fixed range

claims: a gig worker earning $80,000 in the 30% bracket who contributes $10,000 to super saves $1,500 in tax (30% marginal rate minus 15% super tax = 15% x $10,000)
whys: The worked example ignores the 2% Medicare levy, which a deductible contribution also reduces. That makes the saving about $1,700, not $1,500. All of these figures are hard-coded.

claims: The annual concessional contributions cap is $30,000.
whys: Hard-coded in prose and not taken from a constant. The cap is indexed, so it needs checking against the ATO for 2026-27, the year the page's tax table uses.

claims: Business deductions from gig work can only be offset against your gig income (or total income if you are a sole trader reporting in your individual tax return).
whys: This reads as self-contradictory: a gig worker is a sole trader reporting in their individual return. It also leaves out the non-commercial loss rules, which decide whether a business loss can be offset against wage income.

claims: Request additional withholding by lodging a PAYG withholding variation with the ATO, or voluntarily increase your withholding amount with your employer.
whys: The ATO's PAYG withholding variation application is used to reduce withholding. You increase withholding by making a written upward-variation agreement with your payer, not by applying to the ATO. Check the wording against the ATO.

claims: Most gig platform workers (Uber drivers, Deliveroo riders, Airtasker providers, freelancers) are classified as independent contractors
whys: A population claim ('most') with no figure or cited source on the page.

claims: Contributions are taxed at 15% in the fund, compared to your marginal rate (which could be 30-45%).
whys: Hard-coded rates. The phrase "could be 30-45%" leaves out the 16% bracket and the Division 293 extra 15% for high incomes. Both should come from lib/constants tax brackets and the contributions tax rate.

claims: Legal Services Award ... at $33.99 an hour or about $67,174 a year

claims: NSW Health pays interns $80,638 a year from the first full pay period on or after 1 July 2025 (IB2026_007, an interim increase pending the NSW Industrial Relations Commission's decision).
NSW Health intern salary of $80,638 from 1 July 2025 (IB2026_007, interim, pending the NSW IRC decision)
whys: This is an interim rate from a bulletin dated 20 January 2026 and backdated to 1 July 2025. By late October 2026 the NSW IRC decision or a 2026-27 rise has probably replaced it. The figure is also hard-coded as 80_638 in the JSX and not held in a data constant.

whys: For part-year residents the ATO sets the threshold as $13,464 plus $4,736 x months resident / 12. That is not a straight pro-rata of $18,200. Part-year residents are also taxed at resident rates on the year's taxable income, not on two split periods.
constants: needs a PART_YEAR_TFT constant in lib/constants/australian-tax.ts

claims: The tax rate on DASP is 35% for non-residents (65% for working holiday makers).
whys: The rates are typed by hand. The 35% rate applies only to the taxed element. The untaxed element is taxed at 45%.
constants: needs a DASP_TAX_RATES constant in lib/constants

claims: Is a working holiday maker a non-resident? Not for tax purposes... Standard non-resident rates only apply if the employer has not registered as an employer of working holiday makers.
whys: A WHM can be a resident or a non-resident for tax, and WHM rates apply either way. An unregistered employer changes only the withholding rate, because the income is still assessed at WHM rates. The figure also comes from WHM_TAX_BRACKETS_2025_26 while the page is labelled FY2026-27.
reviewerNotes: I agree with the writer's fact question on the working holiday maker answer. A WHM can be a resident or a non-resident for tax, and an unregistered employer changes only the withholding rate. The figure also comes from WHM_TAX_BRACKETS_2025_26 while the page is labelled FY2026-27. These are human decisions, so the text is unchanged.

claims: residents benefit from the $0 tax-free threshold
whys: The resident tax-free threshold is $18,200 (taxed at 0%), not $0. The intended wording is probably 'the 0% rate on the $18,200 tax-free threshold'. I left it because changing it would change a number.

claims: Non-residents also cannot access ... the Medicare levy exemption benefit that residents receive.
The lowest marginal rate for non-residents is 30% ... 0% for residents earning below $18,200 ... residents earning between $18,201 and $45,000 (hard-coded $18,200, $700, 30%, $45,000)
whys: This contradicts line 103, which says non-residents are fully exempt from the Medicare levy. Residents do not receive a levy exemption. The point is probably that non-residents lose Medicare benefits (bulk billing, PBS), as the line 143 bullet explains.

These figures are typed literals rather than TAX_FREE_THRESHOLD, the LITO constant and NR[0].rate. They will go stale when the constants change. Line 70 has the same problem with the $135,000 boundary, which is NR[0].max.
reviewerNotes: I confirmed the flag. 'the Medicare levy exemption benefit that residents receive' contradicts line 103 and the locked heading on line 143 ('No Medicare levy exemption'). The intended meaning is 'no Medicare access'.

claims: No Medicare levy exemption (bullet heading in the list of benefits non-residents lose)
whys: Non-residents ARE exempt from the levy. The bullet body actually describes losing access to Medicare services. The bold heading (locked) is misleading and should be something like 'No Medicare access'.

claims: No tax-free threshold costs up to {formatAUD(TAX_FREE_THRESHOLD * SECOND_BRACKET_RATE)} in additional tax at the 15% marginal rate
No tax-free threshold costs up to formatAUD(TAX_FREE_THRESHOLD * SECOND_BRACKET_RATE) in additional tax at the 15% marginal rate
whys: A non-resident pays 30% (NR[0].rate) on the first $18,200 where a resident pays 0%. That makes the extra cost TAX_FREE_THRESHOLD * NR[0].rate, not * SECOND_BRACKET_RATE. The current formula understates it by half.
The writer's flag holds. A non-resident pays NR[0].rate (30%) on the first $18,200, so the 'up to' figure is understated. Confirm the intended formula (TAX_FREE_THRESHOLD * NR[0].rate) in code.
reviewerNotes: I confirmed the writer's flag. The extra cost is computed as TAX_FREE_THRESHOLD * SECOND_BRACKET_RATE, while a non-resident pays NR[0].rate (30%) on that slice. The source must be fixed outside this pass.

claims: This exemption saves a non-resident earning $100,000 a total of $2,000 per year compared to a resident without private health insurance.
whys: The 2% Medicare levy is payable whether or not a resident has private health insurance (insurance only affects the surcharge), so that qualifier is misleading. The $2,000 is also hard-coded rather than calculateMedicareLevy(100_000).

claims: Both employees receive superannuation at 12% ($10,800)
whys: The figures are hard-coded rather than taken from SUPER_GUARANTEE.rate. Also, line 122 calls the person an 'IT contractor', and a genuine contractor is not automatically owed SG. The example should say employee.

claims: Non-residents can claim a 'Foreign Income Tax Offset' (FITO) in their home country for Australian tax paid, or claim an offset in Australia for tax paid overseas
whys: FITO is Australia's own offset; a home country gives its own foreign tax credit. Also, non-residents are not taxed in Australia on foreign income, so they generally have no Australian FITO claim.

claims: A non-resident receiving dividends from an Australian company typically faces a withholding rate of 15% under most DTAs, reduced from the standard 30% domestic rate.
whys: Fully franked dividends paid to non-residents are exempt from dividend withholding tax. The 30%/15% rates apply to the unfranked portion only, which the sentence does not say.

claims: WHMs are not subject to standard non-resident rates, provided their employer registers as an employer of working holiday makers with the ATO.
whys: WHM rates apply to working holiday taxable income at assessment whether or not the employer registers. Registration only changes the withholding rate (15% vs 30%). As written, the sentence makes the tax rate depend on employer registration.

claims: Refunds are paid to an Australian bank account or a nominated overseas account
whys: The ATO pays refunds into Australian financial institution accounts and does not deposit into foreign bank accounts. This needs checking against ATO guidance.

claims: The ATO will review your objection and issue a decision, typically within 60 days.
Objections must be lodged within 2 years of the assessment date for individuals.
whys: The ATO's published service standard for finalising objections is 56 days (after it has all the information it needs). 60 days is the period after which a taxpayer can give notice requiring a decision. The two are different things, and the figure is hardcoded.

The 2-year period covers individuals with simple tax affairs. Others get 4 years, which the amendment paragraph at line 175 already says. The objection sentence reads as if 2 years covers every individual.

claims: Result row: Refund (if negative) or Amount Owing (if positive)
whys: EX_RESULT = EX_WITHHELD - EX_TOTAL is positive and is shown as 'Refund'. The sign convention in the locked description cell does not match the example beside it.
reviewerNotes: The writer's factQuestions are valid and I am passing them on unchanged: (1) the '60 days' objection figure, against the ATO's 56-day standard; (2) the 2-year objection period, which applies only to simple tax affairs; (3) 'revised payment summary', which looks out of date since STP income statements; (4) the locked 'Refund (if negative)' sign convention, which contradicts the positive EX_RESULT shown as Refund; (5) the hardcoded '2 weeks', which duplicates RETURN_2026.onlineRefundTypical; (6) the table header shows a $90K salary but taxable income of $87,000, and the implied deductions are never stated.

claims: It is typically available within 2 weeks of electronic lodgement
whys: This duplicates RETURN_2026.onlineRefundTypical as a hardcoded value. It is correct today but will drift if the constant changes.

claims: Any surplus in the running cost account at lease end is refunded to the employee.
whys: Leasing providers handle an end-of-lease surplus in different ways. It is often paid back through payroll as taxable salary or put towards the residual. As written, the sentence reads like a fixed rule and does not mention the tax treatment.
constants: lib/constants/novated-lease.ts (none at present; needs a sourced statement)

claims: Used car novated leases deliver smaller GST savings (no GST credit on private-sale used cars)
whys: This is unsourced provider and tax detail in the same answer as the age-limit claim the writer already flagged. It should be checked against the ATO GST guidance on novated leases.

claims: No. A novated lease does not reduce the super your employer must pay ... your employer must work out your super on your pre-sacrifice salary.
whys: The answer now states the rule definitively. It depends on the Payday Super qualifying-earnings rule, but the FAQ cites no constant. The owner should confirm the rule against the source in lib/constants/ote-salary.ts or australian-tax.ts, and check that the maximum contribution base needs no mention.

claims: A smaller post-tax portion covers the employee contribution (also table cell line 147: 'Pre-tax + small post-tax component')
whys: Under ECM the post-tax contribution is 20% of the GST-inclusive base value each year (lines 233, 355). On the page's own $40,000 example that is $8,000 of the $12,000 budget, so the post-tax part is the larger share, not the smaller one. The intro was written as 'partly before tax and partly after tax' so it does not repeat the claim.
reviewerNotes: I agree with the writer: on the page's own example the post-tax ECM contribution is the larger share, so 'A smaller post-tax portion' at line 57 (and the 'small post-tax component' table cell at line 147) looks wrong. Also, line 59 offers 'return the vehicle to the dealer', which conflicts with line 275. Both are passed through as factQuestions and the source was not changed.

claims: At lease end you can ... or return the vehicle to the dealer
whys: This conflicts with line 275 on the same page (pay the residual, refinance it, or trade the car in and start a new lease). A novated lease has no hand-back option without paying out the residual.

claims: less beneficial for employees earning under $45,000, those within 2 years of retirement ... most leasing providers offer portability and payout options
whys: Editorial judgement stated as fact under a heading about eligibility. The FAQ says there is no legislated income minimum. The 2-year retirement figure and the 'most providers' claim have no source. AUDIT is factual-structured, so this cannot be labelled as opinion in this pass.

claims: Most leasing companies offer a portability guarantee ... within 60 to 90 days. No early termination fee applies when transferring ... discount for early settlement typically worth 1 to 3 months of interest
whys: These are industry claims and figures with no cited source. 'No early termination fee applies' is stated as a universal rule.

claims: Registration & CTP $400 a year; 'Varies by state, NSW and VIC are highest'
whys: $400 a year for registration plus CTP looks low for NSW or VIC, where CTP alone usually costs more. The example table figures (7.5% interest, $1.85/litre fuel, 20 to 30% insurance discount at line 88) are hard-coded and unsourced.
constants: none; example budget is inline in the page

claims: someone on 37c in the dollar than to someone on 15c
whys: Correct for 2026-27, but the rates are typed into the prose rather than read from TAX_BRACKETS like the FAQ file does. They will go stale on 1 July 2027 when the bottom rate changes.

claims: The employer is registered for GST and claims credits on the lease payments and packaged running costs.
whys: This is stated as a universal fact, but not every employer is registered for GST or able to claim input tax credits (for example, entities making input-taxed supplies). The rest of the sentence already hedges how much reaches the budget, and this first sentence should probably be made conditional or sourced.

claims: earnings for the $190,100 high income threshold
whys: The figure is correct today and matches HIGH_INCOME_THRESHOLD.current. But it is typed into the FAQ by hand, so it will go stale at the 1 July re-index while the page body (which reads the constant) updates. Line 21 hard-codes '12% super guarantee' the same way, instead of using SUPER_GUARANTEE.rate.

claims: The Clerks, Hospitality, Manufacturing, Security and SCHADS awards give time off hour for hour ... TOIL not taken within the award's window (usually 6 months) must be paid out at the overtime rate.
TOIL not taken within the award's window (usually 6 months) must be paid out at the overtime rate.
whys: lib/constants/time-in-lieu.ts says SCHADS has a 3-month window and pays untaken TOIL at the rates applying when it is paid out, not at the overtime rate. The answer lists SCHADS and then gives a payout rule that does not hold for it.

Confirmed: lib/constants/time-in-lieu.ts lines 23-25 say SCHADS has a 3-month window (cl 28.2(d)) and pays untaken TOIL at the rates applying when payment is made. The answer lists SCHADS by name, so the payout rule is wrong for it.
constants: lib/constants/time-in-lieu.ts (SCHADS entry, windowMonths: 3 and its note)

claims: The annualised salary must exceed the total of base pay plus all penalties the employee would otherwise receive.
whys: Award annualised wage clauses require the salary to be at least what the employee would have earned under the award (no less than). They do not require it to exceed that amount. 'Must exceed' overstates the test.

claims: Employees who do work public holidays receive penalty rates of 2.0x to 2.75x depending on their award.
whys: The multipliers are typed in prose and not taken from the award constants, so they can go stale and cannot be checked against the code.
constants: award penalty constants (e.g. RETAIL_PENALTIES / HOSPITALITY_PENALTIES public holiday fields)

claims: Evening / Afternoon Shift 1.15x - 1.25x and Night / Early Morning 1.15x - 1.3x (generic 'When Do Penalty Rates Apply?' table)
whys: The callout at line 179 on the same page says hospitality evening and night work is a flat cash amount, not a multiplier, and that guides printing 1.15x are wrong. The generic table prints 1.15x anyway. The table cells are locked, so the contradiction stays.
constants: HOSPITALITY_PENALTIES.eveningPerHour / nightPerHour and RETAIL_PENALTIES.eveningAfter6pm in lib/constants/hospitality-award.ts
reviewerNotes: I agree with the writer's fact questions. These are the generic table's 1.15x hospitality multipliers (they contradict the line 179 callout), the abolished 4-yearly award review and 'then renegotiated' at line 262, '12 months' for casual conversion and two old changes listed as FY2026-27 changes (lines 331-332), the 7.6-hour daily trigger at line 146, '5 key factors' versus s62(3) at line 310, and the unsourced population and threshold claims at lines 204, 246 and 319.

claims: Casual conversion pathway changes ... convert to permanent employment after 12 months (listed as a FY2026-27 change)
whys: This conflicts with line 304: the employee choice pathway has applied since 26 August 2024, after 6 months (12 months for a small business employer). It is also not a FY2026-27 change. Line 331 (Right to Disconnect, August 2024 and August 2025) is also listed as a FY2026-27 change but is older.
constants: hard-coded list item; should match the casual conversion text at line 304

claims: Overtime is triggered when a full-time employee exceeds 38 ordinary hours per week or 7.6 hours per day (for a 5-day week)
whys: 7.6 hours is the average day of a 38-hour week, not the award trigger. Awards set their own daily ordinary-hours limits, and the General Retail award allows ordinary shifts longer than 7.6 hours, so stating 7.6 hours as the daily trigger looks wrong.
constants: EMPLOYMENT.standardWeeklyHours plus award-specific daily ordinary hours (not in constants)

claims: The Fair Work Act ... requires consideration of 5 key factors to determine reasonableness
whys: Fair Work Act s62(3) lists about ten matters (a) to (j), not 5. The bullet list at lines 312-318 shows only five of them.
constants: hard-coded; source is Fair Work Act s62(3)

claims: most awards recognise 5 distinct penalty periods
whys: This is an unsourced count about 'most awards'. Hospitality uses flat cash amounts for evening and night work, not periods with multipliers.

claims: 30% marginal rate for $45,001 to $135,000, 2% Medicare levy, 1.25x Saturday and 1.5x Sunday (lines 238, 240, 247, 330, 334)
whys: The figures are correct for FY2026-27 but are typed into the text instead of coming from the tax and award constants, so they will drift at the next change.
constants: tax bracket and MEDICARE_LEVY constants in lib/constants/australian-tax.ts; RETAIL_PENALTIES.saturday/sunday

claims: Emergency service workers, healthcare professionals, and essential infrastructure employees face different reasonableness thresholds
whys: This is an unsourced claim. s62(3) weighs the nature of the role and the needs of the workplace, but it sets no separate thresholds for named groups.

claims: If you have other income that year, 15% may not be enough.
whys: The 15% is typed by hand, but the same paragraph renders it from PPL_RULES.defaultWithholding. If the constant changes, this sentence will go stale.

claims: On {NOW.days} days at the 2026-27 rate ...
whys: '2026-27' is hard-coded, but the figure uses RATE = PPL_RATES[PPL_CURRENT_FY]. The label will be wrong when PPL_CURRENT_FY rolls over.

claims: Schedule 2 (no TFN)
whys: The schedules table on the same page (line 294-295) says Schedule 2 (NAT 1013) covers horticulture and shearing workers, and the no-TFN rates sit inside Schedule 1 (line 291). The ordered list contradicts the table.
constants: Hard-coded in the page; a shared PAYG schedules list in lib/constants/payg-withholding.ts would stop the two drifting

claims: Net pay is the gross amount minus PAYG withholding, minus superannuation (paid separately at the SG rate of 12%)
whys: The employer pays SG on top of ordinary time earnings. It is not taken out of the employee's gross pay unless the salary is quoted as a package. The 12% is also typed in, not taken from the SG constant.

claims: Withheld tax is paid monthly (over $25,000 a year) or quarterly (smaller withholders) via the BAS
whys: This leaves out large withholders (over $1 million a year), who pay electronically within days of each pay and do not report on the BAS. The $25,000 threshold is typed in.
constants: PAYG withholder-size thresholds, which belong in lib/constants/payg-withholding.ts

claims: Claiming the tax-free threshold reduces your weekly withholding by approximately $67
whys: The figure is typed in and the gap between the two scales changes with income and financial year. It should be worked out with withholdingForPeriod(gross, 'weekly', 'noTft') minus withholdingForPeriod(gross, 'weekly', 'tft') at a stated gross.

claims: Common reasons for a withholding variation include ... salary sacrifice arrangements that reduce assessable income; example '$5,000+ in tools or uniforms'
whys: Salary sacrifice already lowers taxable gross through payroll and does not need a section 15-15 variation. The $5,000 example has no source.
constants: None; confirm against the ATO PAYG withholding variation page

claims: Study loan repayment rates range from 1% to 10% depending on your assessable income bracket
whys: This looks out of date. From 2025-26 the HELP/STSL compulsory repayment is a marginal system on repayment income above the threshold, not a 1% to 10% share of total income. It is also based on repayment income, not assessable income.
constants: HELP/STSL repayment constants (the module used by /hecs-help-calculator/)

claims: each additional dollar of gross pay is taxed at a higher marginal rate; net corresponds to a gross of approximately $1,500 (or $78,000 per year)
whys: Under progressive rates, only income above each bracket threshold is taxed at the higher rate, not every extra dollar. $1,500 is exact, not approximate, because example1500 is worked out from 1_500, and $1,500 and $78,000 are typed in rather than rendered with formatAUD.

claims: PAYG instalments threshold to enter: tax liability of $1,000+
whys: This is a locked table cell and it is incomplete. For individuals, the ATO entry test also needs instalment income of $4,000 or more, and notional tax must be $1,000 or more.
constants: None; check the ATO PAYG instalments entry rules

claims: Failing to supply a valid TFN within 28 days triggers the top marginal rate of 47% from dollar one
whys: 47% is the no-TFN rate for residents only. The ATO no-TFN rate for foreign residents is 45%, and the 47% is typed in rather than taken from a constant.

claims: Someone on $90,000 gets the 32% rate ... similar to the 32% marginal rate ... Someone already above $180,000 ... (also line 172: 32%, 17%, $180,000, 47%)
whys: The figures are correct for 2026-27, but they are typed into the prose by hand. WHOLE_OF_INCOME_CAP and ETP_RATES exist and already drive the table and KeyFigures. If those constants are updated, this prose will go stale.
reviewerNotes: I agree with the writer's factQuestion. The figures 32%, $180,000 and 'top rate' in the line 136 prose, and 32%, 17%, $180,000 and 47% in the line 172 methodology, are typed in by hand. ETP_RATES and WHOLE_OF_INCOME_CAP should drive them. The values are correct for 2026-27, so nothing was changed.

claims: The thresholds have risen every year since 2022-23, when the singles threshold was $90,000. Family thresholds rise $1,500 for each dependent child after the first.
whys: The figures look correct, but they are typed into the prose. The FAQ file takes the same child increment from MLS_CHILD_INCREMENT, so this paragraph will drift when the constant changes.
Typed figures. The FAQ takes the child increment from MLS_CHILD_INCREMENT, so the page and the FAQ will drift apart when the constant changes.
constants: MLS_CHILD_INCREMENT in lib/constants/medicare-levy-extra.ts; a historical singles threshold constant in lib/constants/medicare-levy-surcharge.ts
reviewerNotes: Writer fact question passed through. The 2022-23 singles threshold of $90,000 and the $1,500 child increment are typed into the prose, while the FAQ file uses MLS_CHILD_INCREMENT. The page can drift when the constants change.

claims: The LHC figures 2% per year, 70% maximum, age 40 and 20% loading are typed into the prose (lines 206 to 212), as is the 2% Medicare levy at line 124.
whys: The FAQ uses LHC_PER_YEAR / LHC_MAX and the hero uses MEDICARE_LEVY.rate, so these figures should come from those constants. LHC_PER_YEAR and LHC_MAX should move into lib/constants/medicare-levy-surcharge.ts.

claims: many awards set a minimum paid shift (for example 4 hours under the Clerks Award)
whys: This is a population claim ('many awards') with no source on the page, and the 4-hour Clerks Award minimum on a public holiday is not backed by any constant I could find. The Clerks Award minimum engagement is usually given as 3 hours for part-time and casual staff, so check the clause.
constants: Clerks Award entry in lib/constants/modern-awards*.ts (minimum engagement / public holiday clause)

claims: many awards set a minimum paid shift (for example 4 hours under the Clerks Award)
whys: I disagree with the writer's question on the figure. The 4-hour Clerks example is backed by lib/constants/modern-awards.ts:686: 'to work on a public holiday, is entitled to not less than 4 hours' pay (cl 24.3(c), 24.4(d))'. The 3-hour minimum the writer recalled is the general part-time and casual engagement rule, not the public holiday clause. What remains open is only the unsourced population claim 'many awards'. It should either be backed by the minimum-engagement or public-holiday clauses in the award constants or narrowed to the awards the site holds data for.
constants: lib/constants/modern-awards.ts (CLERKS_AWARD notes, line 686) and the per-award minimum engagement notes in lib/constants/modern-awards*.ts

claims: Fortnightly pay calculator item: 'most public service payrolls pay fortnightly, and the classification tables above are published as fortnightly rates.'
'the classification tables above are published as fortnightly rates'
whys: ClassificationBand stores 'Full-time annual salary in dollars' (lib/data/public-service-pay/types.ts line 63) and the schedule tables render annual salaries, so on all 9 jurisdiction pages the tables are not fortnightly rates. 'Most public service payrolls' is also a population claim with no cited source. Suggest: 'most public service payrolls pay fortnightly; this converts the annual salaries above to fortnightly net pay'.
ClassificationBand.annual is the full-time annual salary (lib/data/public-service-pay/types.ts line 63-64), and the tables show annual figures, so this statement is false.
reviewerNotes: Confirmed the writer's flag. ClassificationBand.annual (lib/data/public-service-pay/types.ts line 63-64) is 'Full-time annual salary', and the tables render annual salaries. The claim that 'the classification tables above are published as fortnightly rates' is therefore wrong on all 9 jurisdiction pages. 'Most public service payrolls' is also unsourced. The owner needs to decide the fix.

claims: the same gross salary is worth more in the APS than in the VPS once the 15.4% employer superannuation contribution is counted
whys: 15.4% is the APS median employer contribution (aps.ts:402-404, and the table on this page says '15.4% (median)'). The prose states it as the APS contribution without 'median'.

claims: Junior phase-in lifts 18-year-olds 'from 70%' and 19-year-olds 'from 80%', then '5 points more each July and December', reaching adult rate on 1 July 2029 (18) and 1 July 2028 (19).
whys: The starting percentages, step size and end dates are typed into the prose while the first step comes from JUNIOR_PHASE_IN. They will drift if the scale or determination changes.

claims: The Annual Wage Review 2026 lifted the national minimum wage and award rates by {AWR_2026_FLOORS.increase}% (4.75%) from 1 July 2026, so the retail level 1 vs NMW gap of {L1.hourly - NMW.hourly} an hour carried over from the previous year.
Annual Wage Review 2026 lifted the national minimum wage and award rates by {AWR_2026_FLOORS.increase}% ... so the gap of {L1.hourly - NMW.hourly} an hour carried over from the previous year.
whys: The NMW went from $948.00 to $1,004.90 a week (EMPLOYMENT.minimumWageWeeklyPrevious to minimumWageWeekly), which is about 6.0%. The brief also says the NMW rose 5.97% while award minimums rose 4.75%. So the NMW did not rise by the award percentage, and the gap narrowed (about $1.60 to about $1.37 an hour at level 1). It did not carry over. The sentence should use NMW.increase for the NMW and drop or recompute the 'carried over' clause.

Confirmed. NMW.increase (lib/constants/minimum-wage.ts:102) computes about 5.97%, while award rates rose 4.75%. Because the NMW rose faster, the level 1 vs NMW gap narrowed and did not carry over. Use NMW.increase for the NMW and recompute or drop the 'carried over' clause.
constants: lib/constants/minimum-wage.ts NMW.increase (computed) vs lib/constants/hospitality-award.ts AWR_2026_FLOORS.increase; EMPLOYMENT.minimumWageWeekly/minimumWageWeeklyPrevious in lib/constants/australian-tax.ts
reviewerNotes: I confirmed the writer's fact question. Line 372 says the AWR 2026 lifted 'the national minimum wage and award rates' by AWR_2026_FLOORS.increase (4.75%) and that the level 1 vs NMW gap 'carried over'. The NMW rose about 5.97% (948.00 to 1,004.90 a week, NMW.increase in lib/constants/minimum-wage.ts:102), so the gap narrowed. The string is unchanged in this pass, which the no-fact-change rule requires. It needs a source fix.

claims: ...where the Hospitality Industry (General) Award pays 85%. (Line 256 also types 60% for a 17-year-old.)

claims: Full-time employees who don't work on the public holiday are entitled to their ordinary pay for the day.
whys: Under the NES (Fair Work Act s116), part-time employees whose ordinary day falls on the public holiday are paid too. Naming only full-time employees understates who is covered.

claims: The Hospitality Industry (General) Award (MA000009) covers "cafes, restaurants, pubs and hotels" and "almost everyone in these two industries" is covered by one of the two awards.
whys: Most restaurants and cafes are covered by the Restaurant Industry Award 2020 (MA000119), not MA000009. Fast Food, Registered and Licensed Clubs and other awards also cover parts of both industries. 'Almost everyone' is also a population claim with no source on the page.

claims: The new lead-in says retail and hospitality workers have these rights under the Fair Work Act and the General Retail Industry Award or the Hospitality Industry (General) Award.
whys: Restaurant and many cafe workers are covered by the Restaurant Industry Award (MA000119), and fast food and club workers by other awards, not MA000009. The rights list (2-hour casual minimum engagement, break table) quotes MA000009 clauses that do not apply to them. Resolve this together with the writer's line 80 coverage question.
reviewerNotes: The rights lead-in now names the General Retail Industry Award and the Hospitality Industry (General) Award instead of 'their respective Modern Awards'. This matches the list items, which cite each award's clauses. But it ties all hospitality workers to MA000009, which is the same coverage concern the writer raised for line 80 (restaurant workers fall under MA000119). The sentence is about 30 words, at the limit. Left in place; see the extra fact question.

claims: Juniors aged 19 get 85% in hospitality against 80% in retail; also line 124 '25% casual loading', line 179 '1 July 2026 award rates', line 216 '2% Medicare levy' and 'MA000004'/'MA000009'.
whys: These figures are typed into the prose instead of coming from the constants used elsewhere on the page (HOSPITALITY_JUNIOR_SCALE, RETAIL_JUNIOR_SCALE, RETAIL_AWARD.casualLoading, operativeFrom, Medicare constant). Correct today but will go stale on the next review.

claims: 0% to $18,200, 15% to $45,000, 30% to $135,000, then 37% and 45%, plus the 2% Medicare levy

claims: Delivery Driver Pay Rate: the $31.30 an hour minimum
whys: The delivery minimum differs by vehicle. $31.30 covers bicycle and e-bike only. Motorcycle or scooter is $31.50 and car or van is $32.00 (17 Aug to 31 Dec 2026), and all rates rise on 1 January 2027. A car-based delivery driver reading this page gets the wrong floor, and the figure goes stale on 1 Jan 2027.

claims: Salary sacrifice specifically refers to redirecting pre-tax salary into superannuation. All salary sacrifice is salary packaging, but not all salary packaging is salary sacrifice.
whys: The ATO uses 'salary sacrifice arrangement' for any benefit taken from pre-tax pay (cars, laptops, super), and treats it as the same thing as salary packaging. This super-only definition is the site's own and looks wrong against ATO usage.
constants: n/a (definition; check against the ATO 'Salary sacrificing for employees' page)

claims: Private sector employees ... Their packaging options are limited to super, novated leases, and portable devices.
whys: This overstates the limit. Private sector employers can also package other FBT-exempt or concessional items, for example work-related items under s58X and minor benefits. The claim reads as an exhaustive rule.
constants: n/a (FBT exemptions list; check against the ATO FBT guide)

claims: A $2,000 laptop packaged at the 30% marginal rate saves $600 in income tax.
whys: The three figures are typed in by hand, not taken from the constants. The saving also leaves out the 2% Medicare levy: at 30% plus the levy the saving is $640, not $600.
constants: Work it out from MEDICARE_LEVY plus the current tax brackets in @/lib/constants, as the worked example already does with calculatePayBreakdown

claims: The Child Support Agency includes RFBA in adjusted taxable income
whys: The Child Support Agency no longer exists under that name. It is now Child Support, part of Services Australia. The page also does not say whether child support counts RFBA in full or at the reduced Centrelink factor used for s57A employers.
constants: Agency name text. If the factor is confirmed, it should sit beside CENTRELINK_FACTOR

claims: When you salary package benefits (other than super), your employer reports the grossed-up taxable value as a Reportable Fringe Benefits Amount (RFBA).
whys: RFBA is reported only when an employee's total taxable value of reportable benefits is over $2,000 in the FBT year (FBT.reportableThreshold). Exempt items such as portable electronic devices (the s58X work-related items) are not reportable at all, so 'any benefit other than super' claims too much.

claims: Salary sacrifice specifically refers to redirecting pre-tax salary into superannuation.
whys: The ATO page the guide cites ('Salary sacrificing for employees') uses salary sacrifice for any arrangement that swaps salary for benefits, such as cars and laptops, not only super. So the line between 'salary sacrifice' and 'salary packaging' drawn here does not match the ATO's own use of the terms.
constants: Prose only (SOURCES_LIST ATO salary sacrificing URL)

claims: Employer-provided education that is sufficiently connected to the employee's current role is an exempt benefit.
whys: Work-related education is usually brought to nil taxable value through the otherwise deductible rule, not listed as an exempt benefit. Check the label against the ATO FBT guide before it is repeated.
constants: Prose only (FBT_CAPS_SOURCES.fbtGuideChapter6 or the ATO FBT guide)

claims: Private sector employers: Salary packaging limited to super, novated leases (with FBT unless EV), and portable devices
whys: The EV FBT exemption covers only zero or low emission cars under the luxury car tax threshold for fuel-efficient vehicles. 'Unless EV' reads as if every EV is exempt.

This bullet leaves out work-related education. The self-education section (line 195) describes education as an exempt benefit with no employer-type limit, so the two parts of the page disagree on whether private sector employees can package work-related education.

claims: Salary sacrifice wins when your mortgage rate is below 5-6%, and extra mortgage payments win when rates are high (also the 'High mortgage interest rate (6%+)' item at salary-sacrifice-vs-mortgage.tsx line 156).
whys: The page's own computed scenario table (30% bracket) shows super ahead at 7% over both 10 years (about $68K vs $56K) and 20 years (about $195K vs $167K). The 5-6% threshold is not supported by the model on the page.
reviewerNotes: I checked the writer's factQuestion against SCENARIOS. At 7%, super comes to about $68K and the mortgage to about $56K after 10 years, and super stays ahead after 20 years. The 'below 5-6%' threshold is contradicted by the page's own table. The writer did not change the claim, so the question stands.

claims: The tax benefit of super "could be 22% to 32% per dollar for those in the 37% or 45% brackets" (repeated as "22 to 32 cents per dollar" at line 145).
whys: The range is internally inconsistent. 22 is 37% minus 15% without Medicare, and 32 is 45% plus the 2% Medicare levy minus 15%. It should be either 22 to 30 cents (no Medicare) or 24 to 32 cents (with Medicare).
constants: Derive from TAX_BRACKETS, CONTRIBUTIONS_TAX_RATE and MEDICARE_LEVY.rate, as the FAQ file already does with cents()

claims: Methodology: 'Mortgage comparisons assume interest savings on a standard variable rate loan.'
whys: The table model actually taxes the same $6,000 at 30% plus the 2% Medicare levy before it goes to the loan, and the 7.5% return is described as the 'long-term average for a balanced/growth fund' with no source. The methodology does not match the code.

claims: Money is 'locked until preservation age (currently 60)'.
whys: 60 is typed into JSX here. The FAQ file derives preservation age from PRESERVATION_AGE_TABLE, so this copy can drift from that constant.

claims: 'If your employer contributes $12,000 in SG, you can salary sacrifice up to {formatAUD(CAP - 12_000)}'
whys: The $12,000 SG example is typed with no link to the SG rate or a salary. It is fine as an illustration, but it should be derived (for example, the SG rate times an example salary) so it stays consistent if the cap or the SG rate changes.

claims: All employees (salaried, hourly permanent and hourly casual) receive the SG from their employer, and there is no minimum earnings threshold.
whys: Employees under 18 who work 30 hours or less a week are not entitled to SG (and private or domestic workers have a similar hours rule). 'All employees' is too wide.

claims: Salary provides income stability, paid leave and predictable budgeting.
whys: Permanent hourly employees get the same NES paid leave. Only casuals miss out, so presenting paid leave as a salary advantage over hourly pay is misleading.

claims: Many salaried employees have 'reasonable additional hours' clauses, and the high income threshold is hard-coded as $190,100 from 1 July 2026.
whys: 'Many' is a population claim with no source. Reasonable additional hours come from the NES (s 62), not only contract clauses. HIGH_INCOME_THRESHOLD is typed in this file with a comment saying no lib/constants entry exists, so it should be checked against the FWC figure and moved into constants.
constants: Add HIGH_INCOME_THRESHOLD to lib/constants (EMPLOYMENT or a fair-work constants file)

claims: Hourly workers with overtime earn higher gross income, pushing them into higher tax brackets.
whys: In this example, both $75,000 and $91,091 fall in the same FY2026-27 marginal bracket (30% from $45,001 to $135,000). Neither worker moves into a higher bracket. The effective rate rises only because more income is taxed at 30%. The sentence was left unchanged and should be reworded to say that more of the income is taxed at the marginal rate.
This confirms the writer's flag. $75,000 and $91,091 both fall in the same 30% FY2026-27 bracket. No bracket changes, and the effective rate rises only because more of the income is taxed at 30%.

claims: Overtime is calculated at 1.5x the base hourly rate for the first 2 hours per day, consistent with most modern awards.
whys: This is an unsourced 'most modern awards' claim. Some awards set the first 3 hours at 1.5x (General Retail, for example), and the hourly pros list on line 169 itself says 'first 2-3 hours'. The 12% SG figure is also hard-coded in the prose instead of coming from a constant.

claims: Where your spouse's taxable income is $6,000 or less the full amount transfers; above that it reduces by 15 cents in the dollar.
Spouse transfer reduces by 15 cents in the dollar above $6,000 (SAPTO_TRANSFER.reductionRate 0.15)
whys: The values match SAPTO_TRANSFER, but they are typed into the text instead of read from the constant. The constants file also notes that the ATO's 2025-26 transfer example uses the 16% lowest rate, so check that 0.15 is the right reduction rate for 2025-26.

lib/constants/sapto.ts labels the year 2025-26, and its own note says the ATO's 2025-26 transfer example uses the 16% lowest rate. 15% applies only from 1 July 2026, so the 2025-26 transfer factor is probably 0.16. This needs an owner decision before the next lodgement season.

claims: Being classified in the wrong schedule is one of the more expensive errors in this award.
Social and community services (Schedule B) rates carry the Equal Remuneration Order, starting at ${formatAUD(L1.weekly, 2)} a week.
whys: This is an unsourced comparative claim inside an FAQ answer that is also used in the FAQPage JSON-LD. It is opinion written as if it were fact.

L1 is 'Level 1 pay point 1'. lib/constants/schads-award.ts (lines 21-26, 59, 78) says the ERO tables start at Level 2 and Level 1 receives no uplift, and FAQ line 101 says the same. So the sentence pairs an ERO claim with a non-ERO figure. Either start the ERO claim at Level 2 pay point 1 (L2.weekly) or say that Schedule B rates from Level 2 carry the ERO.
constants: lib/constants/schads-award.ts SCHADS_SACS (Level 2 pay point 1 row); schads-award-faqs.ts L2
reviewerNotes: There is an existing contradiction that the writer did not create. The SACS vs home care answer says 'Social and community services (Schedule B) rates carry the Equal Remuneration Order, starting at ${L1.weekly}'. But L1 is Level 1 pay point 1. The constants header (lib/constants/schads-award.ts lines 21-26) and the FAQ at line 101 both say Level 1 receives no ERO uplift. Raised as a fact question.

claims: set at 4.9% of the standard rate under clause 25.7(d)

This is the only SCHADS rate that is not in lib/constants/schads-award.ts. It also drives the ERO uplift percentage and the annual-difference figures. This confirms the writer's flag.

Super guarantee is paid by the employer on top of wages and is not taken out of take-home pay. This confirms the writer's flag.

claims: Schedule G translation rates affect home care aged-care employees covered on or before 31 December 2024
whys: Date is typed into prose, not taken from a constant. It should come from the same source as the SCHADS_UNVERIFIED notes.

whys: The code says otherwise. TAKE_HOME_SALARIES keeps only multiples of $5,000 ($20k to $200k, then $250k, $300k, $400k and $500k). I confirmed this in the code. TAKE_HOME_SALARIES (lib/data/salary-pages/index.ts, around lines 69-74) is SALARY_GRID filtered to multiples of $5,000, and the $1k pages 301 to the nearest kept page. The note should read its step and ceiling from TAKE_HOME_SALARIES, for example '$5,000 steps from $20,000 to $200,000, then $250k, $300k, $400k and $500k'.
constants: TAKE_HOME_SALARIES in calc-boiler/lib/data/salary-pages/index.ts (lines 69-74); the note should read its step and ceiling from there
reviewerNotes: The first sentence was narrowed correctly to 'Each salary in the table links to a take-home pay page'. The second sentence still says take-home pages exist 'for every $1,000 up to $150,000', which is false. TAKE_HOME_SALARIES in lib/data/salary-pages/index.ts keeps only $5,000 multiples ($20k to $200k, then $250k, $300k, $400k and $500k). I confirmed the writer's fact question. The numbers cannot be changed in this pass, so the claim is left as it is and flagged.

claims: Stage 1: Low and Middle Income Tax Offset (LMITO) introduced, worth up to $530
Stage 1: LMITO introduced, worth up to $530
whys: $530 was the LMITO maximum as first announced in the 2018-19 Budget. It was raised to $1,080 (2019) and then to $1,500 for 2021-22. The table gives the original figure with no note, so readers may take it as the offset's real value. This is a locked table cell.

This confirms the writer's flag. $530 was the maximum first announced in 2018-19. It was raised to $1,080 (2019 Budget, backdated to 2018-19) and was $1,500 for 2021-22. The locked table cell has no note explaining this.
constants: Hard-coded table cell; there is no LMITO constant. Confirm against the ATO LMITO page.

claims: If each job individually pays under the threshold, neither withholds STSL
whys: The ATO STSL component tables use different (lower) earnings thresholds when the employee has not claimed the tax-free threshold. A second job (no tax-free threshold claimed, study loan declared) can therefore withhold STSL below the annualised threshold. Please verify against ATO Schedule 8 before keeping this as a definite rule. The same claim is at stsl-on-payslip.tsx line 149: '(no STSL withheld if each job is under the threshold)'.

This confirms the writer's flag. ATO Schedule 8 uses different STSL thresholds when no tax-free threshold is claimed, so a second job can withhold STSL below the annualised threshold. The same claim is at stsl-on-payslip.tsx line 149.
constants: ATO Schedule 8 (STSL component tax tables). No constant in lib/constants holds the no-tax-free-threshold STSL thresholds.

claims: the co-contribution is paid directly into your super fund, usually within 60 days of your tax return being processed
whys: The 60-day timing has no source on the page. The ATO pages cited do not obviously give this figure, and the payment also depends on the fund reporting the contribution. The same claim is repeated at modules/guide/super-co-contribution.tsx line 83.

claims: This produces a linear phase-out from $500 to $0 across the $15,000 income range.
whys: $500 and $15,000 are hard-coded literals. They should come from CO_CONTRIBUTION (maxEntitlement, HIGHER minus LOWER) so the text stays in sync when the thresholds are indexed.

claims: Under Payday Super contributions should land within roughly a fortnight of each payday
the liability does not lapse quietly with time
whys: The deadline is SUPER_GUARANTEE_CHARGE.current.businessDaysToPay (7 business days), which is about 9 to 11 calendar days. It is 20 business days (about four weeks) for new employees or a new fund. 'Roughly a fortnight' overstates the standard deadline and understates the extended one. Consider rendering the business-day constants here instead.

The writer's flag holds. SUPER_GUARANTEE_CHARGE.current.businessDaysToPay is 7 business days, and businessDaysNewEmployee is 20. The answer should render those constants instead of 'roughly a fortnight'.
No source in this file backs it. The ATO's amendment and limitation period for SGC assessments should be confirmed before this wording is made any stronger.
reviewerNotes: I agree with the writer's fact question. 'Roughly a fortnight' does not match businessDaysToPay = 7, and it misstates the 20-business-day extended deadline. The text was left unchanged because the brief allows no new numbers.

claims: a public holiday anywhere in Australia removes a day nationally
whys: No constant or cited source backs this. The ATO's Payday Super business-day definition should be checked to confirm whether any state or territory public holiday excludes the day nationally, or only a holiday that applies in the relevant place.
The writer's flag holds. No constant or sourceUrl backs this business-day definition, so it should be checked against the ATO Payday Super guidance.
constants: none (could be added to SUPER_GUARANTEE_CHARGE.current with a sourceUrl)

claims: No ATO-initiated assessment ... removes 20 percentage points ... A voluntary disclosure ... removes up to 40 more (line 147); unpaid for 28 days ... a further 28 days and 'previous 24 months' (line 181)
whys: These figures are typed into the JSX, not rendered from constants. They match the comments in SUPER_GUARANTEE_CHARGE.current, but if the schedule changes they will drift from the uplift table.

claims: A public holiday anywhere in Australia removes a day nationally, so a state you do not operate in can still move your deadline.
whys: Check this against the Payday Super business-day definition in QC105846. The statutory wording may cover only a public holiday for a whole state or territory, so a part-state holiday such as a metro-only one would not count. If so, 'anywhere in Australia' is too wide. Not changed.
constants: SUPER_GUARANTEE_CHARGE.current (add a businessDayDefinition field sourced from QC105846)

claims: Most Australian employees have the legal right to choose their own superannuation fund.
whys: This is a population claim with no source on the page. Some employees covered by certain enterprise agreements or defined benefit funds have no choice of fund.

claims: You can lodge the [unpaid super] complaint anonymously.
whys: I believe the ATO unpaid super enquiry asks for your identifying details so it can follow up. The ATO keeps your identity from the employer, but the enquiry itself is not anonymous. Please check this against the ATO page.

claims: The ATO lists performance, Christmas, sign-on and referral bonuses as part of qualifying earnings.
whys: I am not certain the ATO lists sign-on and referral bonuses as ordinary time or qualifying earnings. Please check the ATO OTE/qualifying earnings list before relying on it.

claims: The fund pays the contributions tax on concessional contributions, plus Division 293 tax if your income plus concessional contributions exceeds the threshold.
whys: Division 293 is assessed to the individual by the ATO, not withheld by the fund. The individual can choose to pay it from super through a release authority. The page's own Division 293 FAQ (line 71) says you can pay it from your fund or from personal funds.
reviewerNotes: Not changed. 'The fund pays ... contributions tax ..., plus Division 293 tax'. Division 293 is assessed to the individual (who can choose to release the amount from super), not paid automatically by the fund. The page's own Division 293 FAQ (line 71) says you can pay from your fund or from personal funds. Constant: none (prose); DIVISION_293 in lib/constants/super-contributions.

claims: Super contributions directly reduce the income tax you pay today through concessional tax treatment ... compared to marginal rates of 30%, 37%, or 45% outside super.
whys: Employer SG does not reduce your income tax, and non-concessional contributions get no tax break. Only salary sacrifice and deductible personal contributions do. The list of marginal rates also leaves out the 15% second bracket from 1 July 2026 (line 533), and in that bracket salary sacrifice saves nothing against the 15% contributions tax. The rates are typed in by hand.
constants: income tax bracket constants in lib/constants/australian-tax.ts; CONTRIBUTIONS_TAX_RATE
reviewerNotes: The writer's six factQuestions are valid and should go forward unchanged: lines 90, 150, 607, 533, 583/600 and 109 (typed rates, 'regardless of hours worked', SGC uplift and components, 'most taxpayers', unsourced fund fees).

claims: Every Australian employer must pay the 12% SG for all employees regardless of earnings level, employment type, or hours worked.
whys: 'Regardless of hours worked' conflicts with the same section's 30-hours-a-week rule for under 18s (line 154) and the exemption for domestic workers under 30 hours (line 160). The 12% is also typed in rather than taken from SUPER_GUARANTEE.rate.

claims: an administrative uplift of up to 60% that falls to nil on voluntary disclosure within 30 days
whys: In SUPER_GUARANTEE_CHARGE.current.upliftSchedule, the uplift is 0 for disclosure within 30 days only when the ATO has made no assessment in the past 2 years. Otherwise it is 20%. The sentence also lists 3 SGC components, but the constant has 4 (choice loading is missing).

claims: Fund-type table: typical fees (industry fund 0.5% to 1.0%, retail fund 0.8% to 1.5%, SMSF $2,000 to $5,000) and SMSF 'Balances above $500K'; line 600 says 'target under 1% p.a.'
whys: None of these figures has a source, and the 1% target is opinion written as a rule. AUDIT is factual-prose, so it cannot be relabelled as editorial judgment in this pass.

claims: Salary sacrifice $5,000 reduces income tax by approximately $1,500 (the $5,000 at the 30% marginal rate) ... taxed at 15% inside super ($750) ... net tax saving of $750

whys: The figures are typed in by hand and leave out the 15% bracket, where the saving is nil, as well as the Medicare levy. The range should be derived from the bracket constants and CONTRIBUTIONS_TAX_RATE.

In the table note at line 281, the FY2021-22 LMITO at $80,000 was $1,500, not $1,080. Line 219 '45% above $190,001' (and line 102) is off by one dollar against TAX_BRACKETS_2025_26[4].min.
